newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Commerce's Daley holds hopes for "fast track".
newsitem.headline: U.S. Commerce's Daley holds hopes for "fast track".

text.p: U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley said on Friday he still hopes the Clinton administration will secure "fast track" authority from Congress this year.

Daley, who is due to leave Saturday for South America on his first trade mission since taking office in January, said that while "fast track" was not indispensable for negotiating new deals, the White House was nevertheless committed to obtaining that legislative authority.
"Our goal is to get 'fast track'. That's the game plan. And I believe this administration will get it sooner than later," he told reporters at the Commerce Department.
Daley pointed out that the United States spent the first few years of the Uruguay Round of negotiations under GATT without "fast track" authority.
Trade pacts signed under that authority cannot be amended by Congress, which must vote them up or down within 60 days.
However, Latin American nations would be wary of starting full blown negotiations with Washington to forge a hemispheric free trade zone unless President Clinton gets "fast track".
Lack of "fast track" has prevented Chile from becoming the fourth partner in the North American Free Trade Agreement formed in 1994 by the United States, Canada and Mexico.

Daley said he felt Republicans and Democrats were still far apart on what negotiating powers "fast track" should include, although U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky continues to seek common ground with leaders in Congress.

Himself a former representative from Illinois, Daley said that matters were further complicated by the fact that about 40 percent of the Republican lawmakers and 25 percent of the Democrats have never voted on a major trade bill.
Chile will be the last stop in Daley's 11-day tour, on which he is taking a team of Commerce officials and about 30 executives from big, mid-size and small U.S. firms.

Their mission will start in Rio de Janeiro, then proceed to Sao Paulo and later to Belo Horizonte, where trade ministers from 34 American nations will meet next Friday to discuss the Free Trade Agreement of the Americas initiative.
Daley's delegation, which will also pass through Buenos Aires, will travel on commercial flights rather than on a U.S. military aircraft or a chartered airliner.
Daley acknowledged that his department would probably save money this way but was reluctant to compare his style with some of his predecessors like the late Ron Brown.
The Commerce Department has drawn fire from Republican critics because some businessmen who traveled on Brown's trade missions made large donations to the Democratic Party.
Brown, a former head of the Democratic National Committee, was killed last year when his military aircraft crashed in Croatia during a trade mission to the Balkans.
